| [LIT-583](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-583.md) | Breakdown of Will | Ainslie (2001), Cambridge University Press. The book-length statement of picoeconomics: hyperbolic discounting makes a person a population of bargaining interests, and will is the recursive bundling of choices into precedents. Unread: registered from the publisher's description and the précis, [LIT-586](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-586.md), which stands in for it. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from the publisher's description and from the outline of the book given in its précis, not read. Not open access: Unpaywall reports no open copy, and no author deposit of the book was found (the author's site, picoeconomics.org, carries the précis and articles, not the book). The owner suggested the précis instead, and it is read and filed as [LIT-586](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-586.md) ([NOTE-443](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-443.md)), which follows the book's three sections and twelve chapters. The book is kept as the citation others reach for. A human with library access could read chapters 5-8 (the bargaining model and its evidence) against the précis. |
| [LIT-586](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-586.md) | Précis of Breakdown of Will | Ainslie (2005), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 28(5), the précis of Breakdown of Will (2001). People and other animals discount delayed rewards hyperbolically, so preferences reverse as a smaller, sooner reward comes near, and a person becomes a population of reward-seeking "interests" that must forestall one another. Willpower is the bundling of future choices by treating the present one as a precedent: an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma, not an organ or a top-down ego. The same recursion predicts the will's costs: legalism, circumscribed "lapse districts", motivated blindness to lapses, and rules that favour countable goals over subtle ones. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-443](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-443.md)), as the substitute for the 2001 book ([LIT-583](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-583.md)), which the owner suggested and which the précis follows chapter by chapter. Worth reading as the shortest complete statement of picoeconomics in Ainslie's own words. Hyperbolic discounting makes preference reverse as a smaller, sooner reward draws near, so a person behaves like a population of "interests" that bargain across time. Will is not a faculty above them but a recursive self-prediction: treating each choice as a precedent "bundles" future rewards, an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma in which "credibility is power". The same mechanism predicts the will's side effects: legalism, "lapse districts", motivated misperception and compulsive over-control. |
| [LIT-587](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-587.md) | The Normative Constitution of Agency | Korsgaard (2014), in Rational and Social Agency: The Philosophy of Michael Bratman (OUP), pp. 190–214. Two conceptions of agency are set side by side: natural (action is movement caused by the right mental state) and normatively constituted (action is movement backed by a unified agent, whose unity is achieved by following norms). Following the categorical and hypothetical imperatives gives action "the form of self-determined efficacy". Choosing maxims under that form constitutes one's practical identity. Self-consciousness of one's own attitudes sets the task of unification. Unity of agency "is an achievement, not a given", so people can literally act together. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-455](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-455.md)), in the author's posted manuscript, not the typeset chapter. Worth reading as the read substitute for Self-Constitution (2009, [LIT-597](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-597.md)), which it summarises and extends, and as Korsgaard's direct engagement with Bratman. Agency is "normatively constituted": an action is a movement "backed by the agent as a whole", and that unity is achieved by following the categorical and hypothetical imperatives, which give action "the form of self-determined efficacy". The content of the maxims we choose under that form constitutes our "practical identities". So "we make ourselves into agents", and unity of agency, individual or collective, "is an achievement, not a given". Argued, not proved; the account of reason as unification is said to be "lifted" from her other work. |

Unread: registered from the contents; the theory is read in Bratman's 2018 essay [LIT-567](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-567.md). | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from the Crossref records of the book and its thirteen chapters, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. | [LIT-593](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-593.md) | Intention, Plans, and Practical Reason | Bratman (1987), Harvard University Press; reissued CSLI 1999. The founding statement of the planning theory of intention. As Bratman summarises it in [LIT-567](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-567.md), prior partial plans "settle practical issues, pose problems of means and the like, filter solutions to those problems, and guide action", supporting cross-temporal and social organisation within our cognitive limits. Unread: registered from catalogue records; the theory is read in the 2018 essay. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from library catalogue records, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. Harvard University Press (1987) and the CSLI reissue (1999) are not open, and the Internet Archive's two scans are access-restricted lending copies, not opened. | [LIT-596](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-596.md) | Three Theories of Self-Governance | Bratman (2004), Philosophical Topics 32(1/2):21–46; reprinted in Structures of Agency (OUP 2007), pp. 222–253. | [LIT-597](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-597.md) | Self-Constitution: Agency, Identity, and Integrity | Korsgaard (2009), Oxford University Press, from her 2002 Locke Lectures. The argument is that we constitute ourselves as agents, and as the particular agents we are, by choosing under the constitutive principles of action, the categorical and hypothetical imperatives. On Plato's "constitutional model", good action is action that issues from a unified soul. The chapters run from agency and identity to "How to be a Person". Unread: registered from the contents; the account is read in [LIT-587](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-587.md). | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from the Crossref records of the book and its ten chapters, not read: no lawful copy of the book could be reached. Per the report's ERIC abstract: routine action runs off by "contention scheduling" among competing schemas, and a "supervisory attentional mechanism" biases that selection for novel, ill-learned, dangerous or planned action; "will becomes the application of attentional resources to the control of action". Unread. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from bibliographic records and from the ERIC abstract of the 1980 technical report, not read. | [LIT-602](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-602.md) | The Intimate Contest for Self-Command | Schelling (1980), The Public Interest, Summer 1980, pp. 94-118. People behave sometimes "as if they had two selves" in "continual contest for control", and the tactics of self-management (removing the option, bright lines, monitoring, delays, raising the stakes) are the tactics of managing someone else. A single-dimension model of impatience fits poorly. Which self is authentic is left open. Failures of consumer self-management may be worth "on the order of a trillion dollars". | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-452](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-452.md)), in place of the 1984 Ely Lecture ([LIT-573](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-573.md)), which has no lawful free copy. Worth reading as Schelling's own first statement of "egonomics": a person sometimes behaves "as if they had two selves" that alternate in command, and the tactics people use on themselves (mittens, alarm clocks across the room, bright lines, Christmas savings, deadlines, delays) are the tactics they use to manage another person. It refuses to say which self is authentic in general, and it gives an order-of-magnitude estimate that failures of consumer self-management cost as much as all other consumer-ignorance problems together. |
| [LIT-603](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-603.md) | The Emperor's New Markov Blankets | Bruineberg, Dołęga, Dewhurst & Baltieri (2020 preprint; BBS 45:e183, 2022). Markov blankets entered variational inference as Pearl's conditional-independence shields, tools on a scientist's map. In the free-energy literature since Friston 2013 they became boundaries in the world between agent and environment: "Friston blankets". The two are different constructs; Friston blankets need extra assumptions (a chosen internal node, sensorimotor labels, steady state, sparse coupling) that the formalism does not supply. Using them for metaphysical conclusions ("inference within a model") requires metaphysical premises; used instrumentally ("inference with a model") they are innocent but philosophically idle. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-447](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-447.md)), but in its December 2020 PhilSci-Archive version; the Behavioral and Brain Sciences target article of 2021–2022 is, by the authors' own note, "heavily rewritten" and could not be read lawfully beyond its abstract. Worth reading as the critique that names the problem: "Pearl blankets", the conditional-independence tool of graphical models, are conflated with "Friston blankets", a realist construct meant to be the boundary between an agent and its world. The second cannot be read off the mathematics of the first, and its use to settle questions about life and mind needs metaphysical premises of its own. It re-runs the primordial-soup simulation of [LIT-526](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-526.md) and shows how the blanket found there depends on modelling choices. |
| [LIT-605](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-605.md) | An Accumulator Model for Spontaneous Neural Activity Prior to Self-Initiated Movement | Schurger, Sitt & Dehaene (2012), PNAS 109(42). In Libet's spontaneous movement task, a leaky stochastic accumulator, δx = (I − kx)Δt + cξ√Δt, with weak constant urgency I and a threshold, fitted only to waiting times, reproduces the averaged readiness potential (r² = 0.96): time-locking to threshold crossings averages up the autocorrelated noise that produced them. Fast responses to random interruptions were preceded by a slow negativity, as predicted. The "neural decision to move now" is the late threshold crossing, about 150 ms before movement, so Libet's inference of an unconscious decision a half-second earlier is unfounded. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-462](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-462.md)); worth reading as the model that reinterprets the readiness potential. A leaky stochastic accumulator with a weak constant input ("urgency"), fitted with three parameters to 14 participants' waiting times in Libet's task, reproduces the shape of the averaged readiness potential (r² = 0.96) because averaging epochs time-locked to threshold crossings recovers the noise that happened to carry the accumulator there. Its prediction, that fast responses to unpredictable clicks are preceded by a slow negativity, was confirmed (13 participants). On this account the "neural decision to move now" is the threshold crossing about 150 ms before movement, not the onset of the readiness potential, and Libet's inference that the brain decides before awareness is "unfounded". The authors say plainly that this shows the readiness potential could reflect spontaneous fluctuation, not that it does. |
| [LIT-684](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-684.md) v3 | Responsibility and Control: A Theory of Moral Responsibility | Fischer & Ravizza (1998), Cambridge University Press. Unread seed. The most influential reasons-responsiveness theory of moral responsibility. Responsibility requires guidance control, not regulative control (the control that involves alternative possibilities), and Frankfurt-type cases show the two come apart. An agent has guidance control of an action when it issues from her own, moderately reasons-responsive mechanism: regularly receptive to reasons, including moral ones, and at least weakly reactive to them. The mechanism is her own when she has taken responsibility for it, which makes responsibility historical. Guidance control so described is compatible with causal determinism, which is the position Fischer calls semicompatibilism. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 as a seed, from Crossref's book and chapter records, the chapter openings Cambridge Core displays, the record's second-hand readings, the SEP entry Moral Responsibility ([LIT-691](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-691.md)) and Fischer's own summary in "Stories and the Meaning of Life" ([LIT-689](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-689.md), read), not read. No lawful full text was found: the book is paywalled at Cambridge Core, and Unpaywall and OpenAlex list no open copy (oa_status closed, no repository holding). The shorter work the record's book rule asks for is the authors' own précis (Philosophy and Phenomenological Research 61(2), September 2000, first page 441, DOI 10.2307/2653660), also closed: JSTOR answered with a bot challenge, so I stopped there. Fischer's UC Riverside pages post no papers that could be reached, and the copies of the précis in two third-party collections of his papers (andrewmbailey.com/jmf and its wixsite continuation) are not the author's, a publisher's or a repository's, so they were not opened. A web search also shows a PDF titled "Fischer Guidance control and RR" on a UNAM institute's site, whose search snippet is the book's series page; it is a course file with no statement of permission, so it was not opened either. A person with Cambridge Core or library access can supply the book (Cambridge UP, 1998, DOI 10.1017/CBO9780511814594); chapters 2, 3 and 8 (pp. 28–91 and 207–239) are the parts to read first, and the short précis is the quickest way to an Active reading. | [LIT-685](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-685.md) v2 | Freedom Within Reason | Wolf (1990), Oxford University Press. Unread seed. | [LIT-687](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-687.md) v3 | Responsiveness and Moral Responsibility | Fischer (1987/88), in Schoeman (ed.), Responsibility, Character, and the Emotions (CUP), pp. 81–106; read in its My Way reprint. Responsibility is historical and compatible with determinism (semicompatibilism). | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-579](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-579.md)): in full, in the reprint in Fischer's My Way (OUP 2006), from Andrew M. | [LIT-688](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-688.md) v2 | Asymmetrical Freedom | Wolf (1980), The Journal of Philosophy 77(3):151–166. Unread. By the SEP's report it is the origin of the Reason View's asymmetry: an agent who acts in accord with the True and the Good is praiseworthy even if psychologically determined so that she could not have done otherwise, but one who acts against it is blameworthy only if she could have done otherwise. Blame therefore needs regulative control and praise needs only guidance control, and Wolf answers the threat from determinism by denying that physical determination entails psychological determination. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from Crossref, the record's own second-hand readings and the SEP entry it already holds, not read. | [LIT-689](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-689.md) | Stories and the Meaning of Life | Fischer (2009), Philosophic Exchange 39(1), pp. 3–15. Section I sketches his framework for moral responsibility: guidance control, not regulative control, is the freedom-relevant condition; it consists in acting from one's own, moderately reasons-responsive mechanism; responsibility is historical and compatible with causal determinism; and the moral of Frankfurt-style cases is that it depends on how the actual sequence unfolds. The paper's thesis is that the value of acting freely is the value of artistic self-expression: free action makes a life a story with narrative value, though the life is judged mainly by moral and prudential standards. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-547](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-547.md)); worth reading as the only first-hand, lawful statement by Fischer that the record holds of his framework for moral responsibility: guidance control, not regulative control, is the freedom-relevant condition; guidance control is mechanism ownership plus moderate reasons-responsiveness; responsibility is historical and compatible with causal determinism; and the moral of Frankfurt-style cases is that responsibility depends on the actual sequence. Its own thesis is that the value of acting freely is the value of artistic self-expression, which gives a life narrative value. It lists the framework's elements without arguing for them. |
| [LIT-690](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-690.md) v2 | Sanity and the Metaphysics of Responsibility | Wolf (1987/88), in Schoeman (ed.), Responsibility, Character, and the Emotions (CUP), pp. 46–62. Unread. JoJo, raised by a vicious dictator, identifies wholly with the values he inherits yet is not responsible, because his upbringing leaves him unable to see right from wrong. What must be added is sanity: the ability to know and appreciate what one is doing and that it is right or wrong. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from Cambridge's chapter record and opening extract, the record's second-hand readings and an MIT lecture handout about the essay, not read. | [LIT-691](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-691.md) | Moral Responsibility | Talbert (2019; revised 2024), Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. A survey of moral responsibility: its relation to free will and determinism, forward-looking, Strawsonian and reasons-responsiveness accounts, the attributability/accountability distinction that grew from Wolf and Watson, the moral competence condition (Wolf's JoJo), conversational views, standing to blame, outcomes, skepticism, moral luck, ultimate responsibility, manipulation and the epistemic condition. Its §2.3 is a page-referenced summary of Fischer and Ravizza's guidance control. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-548](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-548.md)); worth reading as the record's map of moral responsibility apart from the free-will question, and as its most exact second-hand source for two accounts the record cannot read first-hand: Fischer and Ravizza's guidance control (§2.3, with page references to the 1998 book) and Wolf's critique of Real Self views and her moral-competence condition, including the JoJo case (§§3.1.1, 3.2). | [LIT-692](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-692.md) | Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person | Frankfurt (1971), The Journal of Philosophy 68(1):5–20. What is essential to a person is the structure of the will. A person's will is the effective first-order desire, the one that moves him "all the way to action" (p. 8). A second-order volition is wanting a desire to be one's will; persons have them, and wantons, who "do not care" about their wills, do not (pp. 10–11). Forming one is identifying with one desire and withdrawing from another (p. 13). Freedom of the will is having the will one wants, "securing the conformity of his will to his second-order volitions" (p. 15), and a decisive identification "resounds" through all higher orders (p. 16). Moral responsibility needs neither a free will nor alternatives: the willing addict acts "of his own free will" (pp. 18–20). | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-545](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-545.md)); worth reading as the source of the hierarchical account of the will, which the record has so far held only second-hand: first- and second-order desires, the will as the effective desire, second-order volitions, wantons and persons, freedom of the will as having the will one wants, decisive identification that "resounds" through higher orders, and a responsibility that needs neither a free will nor alternatives. Read it knowing that it is short and programmatic, that identification is stated, not analysed, and that it already contains both the decisive commitment (p. 16) and the acceptance of an addict made by another (n. 10), which the record's surveys date later. |

| [LIT-694](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-694.md) | Alternate Possibilities and Moral Responsibility | Frankfurt (1969), The Journal of Philosophy 66(23):829–839. The principle of alternate possibilities (PAP), "a person is morally responsible for what he has done only if he could have done otherwise", is false. Coercion excuses only when the agent acts because of it (§§II– III). Black, ready to make Jones4 act as he wants and never needing to, shows that circumstances can make an action unavoidable without playing any role in bringing it about (§IV); such a fact "does not help in any way to understand" the action and cannot excuse it (§V). PAP should be replaced by: not responsible "if he did it only because he could not have done otherwise", which "does not appear to conflict" with compatibilism (pp. 838–839). | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-546](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-546.md)); worth reading as the origin of Frankfurt-style cases and the shortest first-hand statement of the argument against the principle of alternate possibilities: a fact that makes an action unavoidable but plays no role in bringing it about cannot excuse, so PAP should give way to "a person is not morally responsible for what he has done if he did it only because he could not have done otherwise" (p. 838). Read it knowing that its case is schematic (Black, Jones4 and "a certain action"; the voting and shooting versions in the record's surveys are later retellings), that its prior sign is in a footnote, and that it leaves "could have done otherwise" and "morally responsible" unanalysed on purpose (n. 1). |

| [LIT-700](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-700.md) | Three kinds of collective attitudes | List (2014), Erkenntnis 79(S9):1601–1622. Collective attitudes come in three kinds. Aggregate attitudes summarise members' attitudes by a rule or a market, supervene proposition-wise and need not be rational. Common attitudes are held by all members with common awareness, matter for coordination, and inherit consistency from their unanimity. Corporate attitudes belong to a group agent, guide its action, supervene holistically on members' contributions and must be rational. The kinds are almost logically independent, and fears and hopes divide the same way as beliefs and desires. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-554](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-554.md)); worth reading as the disambiguation the collective-attitudes literature needs: aggregate attitudes (summaries, supervening proposition by proposition), common attitudes (unanimous and commonly known, supervening on a slightly enriched base) and corporate attitudes (a group agent's, supervening holistically and not straightforwardly reducible). The three are almost logically independent. A review by its own description, with no new theorem; its value for this record is that it names fears and hopes among the attitudes the split applies to, which gives the collective-emotion debate a vocabulary. |
| [LIT-705](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-705.md) | Group Agency and Supervenience | List & Pettit (2006), Southern Journal of Philosophy 44(S1):85–105. A group agent's rationality must supervene on its members' contributions, but not proposition by proposition. Three impossibility results show that robust group rationality (complete, consistent, deductively closed group judgments for every profile of rational member judgments) is inconsistent with majoritarian, uniform proposition-wise and proposition-wise supervenience. Premise-based and distributed premise-based procedures show it is consistent with set-wise supervenience, with group judgments that can be discontinuous with the members' judgments on the same proposition. Emergent agency without any member's conception of the group is set aside as unintelligible. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-550](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-550.md)); worth reading as the short, formal core of List and Pettit's group agency: a group can be a robustly rational judge only if its judgment on a proposition is not, in general, a function of its members' judgments on that proposition. Group judgments supervene on members' judgments set-wise, not proposition-wise, so a group agent is individualistically unmysterious and still "not directly continuous" with its members. Read here as the lawful substitute for the unread book [LIT-391](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-391.md), whose chapter 3 takes up the same supervenience question; the impossibility results are cited from other papers, not proved here. |
| [LIT-718](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-718.md) | The Conversable, Responsible Corporation | Pettit (2017), in Orts & Smith (eds), The Moral Responsibility of Firms, OUP, pp. 15–35. Corporations are agents and, through authorised spokespersons, conversable ones that avow attitudes and make promises. Because majority voting on connected judgments can be inconsistent, a conversable corporation must correct its aggregate and so forms a mind of its own. Conversable agents are fit to be held responsible, so corporations are. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-569](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-569.md)): in full, from the manuscript Pettit circulated for a master class at the European University Institute. Worth reading as the short statement of his case that corporations are fit to be held responsible. A corporation is a conversable agent: it speaks for itself through authorised spokespersons and commits itself, rather than reporting its members' attitudes. It must correct for the inconsistency any mechanical aggregation produces, so it has a mind of its own. Conversable agents meet the three conditions of fitness to be held responsible. The chapter stands in for the unread 2007 paper [LIT-742](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-742.md). |
| [LIT-727](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-727.md) | The Corporation as a Moral Person | French (1979), American Philosophical Quarterly 16(3):207–215. A moral person is a non-eliminable subject of accountability, which requires intentional agency. A corporation's Internal Decision (CID) Structure, its organizational chart plus recognition rules in corporate policy, licenses redescribing members' acts as corporate acts done for corporate reasons. So corporations, unlike mobs, can be full-fledged moral persons. That agency suffices for moral personhood is asserted, not argued here. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-568](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-568.md)): in full, from a scanned JSTOR copy in a Brooklyn College instructor's readings folder. Worth reading as the founding statement of the claim that corporations are moral persons. French rests it on the Corporate Internal Decision (CID) Structure: an organizational chart plus recognition rules embedded in corporate policy. It licenses redescribing members' acts as corporate intentional acts. Limits: he asserts, and says he cannot here argue, that intentional agency suffices for moral personhood, and the paper offers no test of corporate intentionality beyond the redescription itself. |
| [LIT-728](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-728.md) | Précis of Responsibility and Control: A Theory of Moral Responsibility | Fischer & Ravizza (2000), Philosophy and Phenomenological Research 61(2):441–445. Moral responsibility requires guidance control, not regulative control over alternatives. Guidance control is acting from a mechanism that is one's own, because one has taken responsibility for it, and that is moderately reasons-responsive: regularly receptive to reasons, some of them moral, and at least weakly reactive. The view is historical and compatible with causal determinism. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-575](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-575.md)): in full, from Andrew M. Bailey's collection of Fischer's papers, used on the owner's instruction. Worth reading as the authors' own five-page statement of the account of Responsibility and Control ([LIT-684](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-684.md)). It says moral responsibility requires only guidance control, which has two parts: the agent's ownership of the mechanism that issues in the action, acquired by taking responsibility for it, and that mechanism's moderate reasons-responsiveness. It summarises and does not argue; the arguments are in the unread chapters. |
| [LIT-730](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-730.md) | Episteme Symposium on Group Agency: Replies to Gaus, Cariani, Sylvan, and Briggs | List & Pettit (2012), Episteme 9(3):293–309. Replies to a symposium on Group Agency. Ecological rationality is classical rationality relative to an environment; robust group rationality can be relaxed by context, yet proposition-wise aggregation stays very limited. Group attitudes are real and non-redundant: role-based member acceptance does not reduce them. Group agents are fit to be held responsible in their own right but should have restricted rights, on normative individualism. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-582](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-582.md)): in full, from the authors' copy on List's LSE pages. Worth reading as the authors' own short commentary on Group Agency ([LIT-391](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-391.md), unread), which it quotes with page references. It says the premise-based procedure was only ever illustrative, that robust group rationality may be relaxed case by case without rescuing proposition-wise supervenience, that no accessible individualistic recipe makes group attitudes redundant, and that group agents are fit to be held responsible in their own right but should have restricted rights. Limits: replies to commentaries not in the record; the book's claims are seen only as quoted. |
| [LIT-742](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-742.md) | Responsibility Incorporated | Pettit (2007), Ethics 117:171–201. Incorporated groups face significant choices, can recognise the relative value of their options, and can choose in sensitivity to those values, so they meet the conditions for being fit to be held responsible. Unread: the argument is read in his 2017 chapter [LIT-718](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-718.md). | Deferred — registered 2026-10-05 from Crossref, not read: no lawful full text could be reached (SSRN's download is blocked to this client, and the journal is closed).
